## Why a dashboard, and why now

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
Your final project deliverable includes a dashboard. This lab gives
you a **working reference example** — built live, in front of you,
including the mistakes — that you can copy from and adapt.
:::

- We'll reuse a model you already know: the VAR system from Lab 4
- The point isn't to teach VAR again — it's to teach how to **display**
  results you've already learned how to produce
- Every dashboard you'll ever build has the same bones: data,
  computation, layout, and (usually) a way for the viewer to interact

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A different kind of lab
Labs 1–5 taught time series methods. This one teaches a **tool**. The
good-coding-practices track (config blocks, error handling) pauses
here — there's no new practice today, just a new skill: presentation.
:::

## What is a dashboard, really?

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
A dashboard is a **report that responds**. A static report shows one
fixed view of your results. A dashboard lets the viewer choose what
they see — which variable, which time period, which model — without
you rebuilding anything.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition
A dashboard is a document organized into cards, arranged in rows and
columns, optionally with controls (dropdowns, sliders) that let the
viewer change what's displayed.
:::

Four moving pieces, in every dashboard you'll ever build:

1. **Data** — what you're showing
2. **Computation** — what you did to it (a model, a test, a summary)
3. **Layout** — how it's arranged on the page
4. **Interactivity** *(optional, but what makes it a dashboard and not
   just a report)*

## Why Quarto, specifically

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
There are other dashboard tools — Streamlit, Dash, Shiny — but they
require a **running server** and a framework you'd need to learn from
scratch.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Quarto dashboards are static
No server. `quarto render` produces a self-contained HTML file — the
same thing that happens when you render a slide deck or the textbook.
Deploy it to GitHub Pages exactly like your Week 4 website.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 1em;"}
Same `.qmd` files, same code cells, same `# %%`-adjacent authoring
experience — just a different `format:` in the YAML.
:::

## Build increment 1 — the skeleton {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## The YAML: one new key

```yaml
---
title: "ECON-5371 Project Dashboard"
subtitle: "Reference example — Vector Autoregression"
author: "Your Name"
format: dashboard
---
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; margin-top: 1em;"}
`format: dashboard` is the only thing that turns a normal `.qmd` into
a dashboard. Everything else about writing code cells stays exactly
what you already know.
:::

## Rows, and your first value boxes

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
`##` headings become **rows**. Inside a row, a code cell with
`#| content: valuebox` becomes a compact stat card.
:::

```{{python}}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Observations"
#| icon: calendar3
#| color: primary
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/macro_var_synthetic.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
dict(value=len(df))
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The mechanic
A value box cell returns a Python `dict` — Quarto reads its keys
(`value`, `icon`, `color`) to build the box. `icon` names come from
the free Bootstrap Icons library.
:::

## What we actually saw when we rendered this

::: {style="font-size: 1.2em; text-align: center; margin-top: 1em;"}
Three value boxes — stretched to fill the **entire screen height**,
not a compact strip.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Why: a dashboard with one row always fills 100%
Quarto splits page height across however many rows exist. With only
one row — even set to `height=20%` — there's nothing else to claim
the remaining 80%, so Quarto expands the one row to fill everything.
This isn't a bug. It's relative sizing with nothing to divide.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
The fix wasn't in this row at all — it was adding a **second row**.
Row heights only make sense relative to each other.
:::

## Build increment 2 — a plot card {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Adding the time-series plot

```{{python}}
#| title: "Output Gap, Inflation, and Policy Rate"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (11, 4)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for var in ["output_gap", "inflation", "policy_rate"]:
    ax.plot(df["date"], df[var], label=var, linewidth=1.2)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Matplotlib doesn't auto-resize
Unlike interactive plotting libraries, a static matplotlib figure
doesn't stretch to fit its card. Set the figure size explicitly —
`plt.rcParams['figure.figsize']` — sized for how wide the card will
actually be.
:::

## Three rows in, cramped again

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
Once we added a **third** row — a table and two value boxes — the
page looked squeezed again. A "Date Range" box even had its text
clipped, cut off mid-number.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Same root cause, compounding
Row 1 and Row 2 had explicit heights (20% / 80%) that summed to 100%
— fine for two rows. Adding a third row with **no height specified**
meant Quarto tried to fit 20% + 80% + (undefined) into one page. The
undefined row got squeezed, and so did everything else.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The fix: audit your total every time you add a row
We rebalanced to 15% / 55% / 30% — three numbers that actually sum to
100%. Every time you add a row to a dashboard, re-check that all your
row heights on that page still add up.
:::

## Build increment 3 — columns and a table {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Splitting a row into columns

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
`###` headings, nested under a `## Row`, split that row into
**columns** — one level down from how rows split the page.
:::

```markdown
## Row {height=30%}

### Column {width=60%}
... stationarity table ...

### Column {width=40%}
... lag order and stability value boxes ...
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Same nesting logic throughout Quarto dashboards: page → rows →
columns → cards. One heading level per layer.
:::

## A results table with `tabulate`

```{{python}}
#| title: "Stationarity (ADF Test)"
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

rows = []
for var in variables:
    result = adfuller(df[var], autolag="AIC")
    verdict = "Stationary" if result[1] < 0.05 else "Unit root"
    rows.append([var, f"{result[0]:.3f}", f"{result[1]:.4f}", verdict])

adf_table = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Variable", "ADF Stat", "p-value", "Result"])
Markdown(tabulate(adf_table, showindex=False, headers=adf_table.columns))
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
`tabulate` turns a small DataFrame into a clean markdown table;
wrapping it in `Markdown(...)` tells Quarto to render it as
formatted text, not print raw markdown syntax to the page.
:::

## One more content problem: text that overflows its box

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
Even after fixing row heights, one value box still showed clipped
text: `"1985–2024"` wrapped onto two lines, and the second line got
cut off by the box's own height.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Value boxes expect short content
A value box is built for a glanceable number or short label — not a
long string. `"1985–2024"` (9 characters) was too wide to stay on one
line at that font size.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The fix: shorten the content, don't fight the box
We changed the display to `'85–'24` — a compact year format that
fits on one line. When a value box's content doesn't fit, shortening
what you're displaying is usually the right move, not resizing the
box indefinitely.
:::

## Build increment 4 — a second page, and tabs {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## Multiple pages: `#` headings

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
A **level-1** heading (`#`, not `##`) starts a new **page** —
appearing as a link in the dashboard's navbar.
:::

```markdown
# Overview
... everything so far ...

# Model Results
... Granger causality, IRFs, FEVD ...
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Confirmed: state carries across pages
Variables defined in Page 1's Python cells (`df`, `variables`) were
still available in Page 2's cells, without re-importing or re-loading
anything. One shared Python session for the whole document.
:::

## Tabs: `.tabset` on a row

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
Three results — Granger causality, impulse responses, variance
decomposition — don't need to compete for space on one page. A
**tabset** lets the viewer click between them.
:::

````markdown
## Row {.tabset height=100%}

```{{python}}
#| title: "Granger Causality"
... table ...
```

```{{python}}
#| title: "Variance Decomposition"
... plot ...
```
````

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
Two cells, `.tabset` on the row — this should produce two tabs.
:::

## What we actually got: four tabs, not three

::: {style="font-size: 1.2em; text-align: center; margin-top: 1em;"}
A dropdown-plus-image pair, meant to be **one** tab
("Impulse Responses"), rendered as **two separate tabs** instead.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Why: `#| title:` labels one cell, not a group
Inside a `.tabset`, **every individual cell** becomes its own tab by
default. `#| title:` names that one cell's tab — it doesn't merge
multiple cells into a single tab, even if you intend them to belong
together.
:::

## The fix: `###` headings group cells into tabs

````markdown
## Row {.tabset height=100%}

### Granger Causality
```{{python}}
... one cell ...
```

### Impulse Responses
```{{ojs}}
... dropdown cell ...
```
```{{ojs}}
... image cell ...
```
````

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
A `###` heading starts a new tab; **every cell underneath it**,
however many, belongs to that same tab. This is the same row → column
→ card nesting pattern from Build Increment 3, one more layer deep.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## General lesson
When a Quarto layout container (tabset, columns, rows) needs to hold
*more than one cell* as a single unit, reach for an explicit heading
to group them — don't rely on a single cell's own title option.
:::

## Build increment 5 — real interactivity {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## What makes this a dashboard, not a report

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em;"}
Everything so far is **static** — the same output every time,
regardless of who's looking at it. A dropdown that changes what's
displayed is the feature that actually earns the word "dashboard."
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Observable JS (`{{ojs}}`)
A second language Quarto supports alongside Python, running in the
viewer's browser — no server required. This keeps a dashboard
deployable as plain static HTML, same as GitHub Pages.
:::

## A dropdown that swaps an image

```{{python}}
#| output: false
# Generate one IRF panel image per shock variable, saved to images/
# (full code: one matplotlib figure per shock, saved as a PNG)
```

```{{ojs}}
viewof shock_choice = Inputs.select(
  ["output_gap", "inflation", "policy_rate"],
  {{label: "Shock to:", value: "output_gap"}}
)
```

```{{ojs}}
html`<img src="images/irf_${{shock_choice}}.png" style="width: 100%;">`
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
`viewof` creates both the visible dropdown **and** a reactive
variable, `shock_choice`. Any `{{ojs}}` cell referencing it re-runs
automatically the moment the dropdown changes.
:::

## Why images, not a live recomputation

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## A deliberate simplification
Connecting Python-computed values directly into `{{ojs}}` (via
`ojs_define()`) is possible, but stacks several new, untested
concepts at once. Pre-generating one image per option and letting the
dropdown just swap which image shows is simpler, safer, and still
genuinely interactive.
:::

This worked on the first render — no gotcha here, for once.

## Build increment 6 — UTEP branding {.section-divider background-color="#87A96B" footer=false}

## A theme file, same pattern as the slides

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
Dashboard theming uses the same SCSS structure as `eo-slides.scss`:
`scss:defaults` for variables, `scss:rules` for fine-grained CSS.
:::

```scss
/*-- scss:defaults --*/
$utep-orange: #FF8200;
$utep-blue:   #041E42;
$utep-silver: #B1B3B3;

@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Crimson+Pro...');

$primary:   $utep-blue;
$secondary: $utep-silver;
$navbar-bg: $utep-blue;
$navbar-fg: #FFFFFF;
```

```yaml
format:
  dashboard:
    theme: [cosmo, dashboard-theme.scss]
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## UTEP's current brand fonts
Crimson Pro for headings and titles, Inter for body text — both
freely available via Google Fonts, so no fallback substitution is
needed.
:::

## Mapping value box colors to the brand

::: {style="font-size: 1.1em;"}
`color: primary` and `color: secondary` now resolve to UTEP Blue and
Silver automatically, once set in the theme file. For Orange — not a
default Bootstrap slot — use the hex value directly:
:::

```yaml
#| color: "#FF8200"
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
Result: every value box on the page uses only Blue, Silver, and
Orange — no leftover Bootstrap cyan or green.
:::
